title: Order service: duplicates, stock, retries, and pages
inspired_by: High-volume commerce teams (for example, Amazon-style order processing). An original simulation, not a real interview question.
summary: A small order service places orders, reserves stock, charges a payment gateway, and lists orders page by page. Customers report double orders and missing orders, and cancelling is not built yet.

followups.problem_understanding: Before writing code, list five questions you would ask about a 'refund an order' feature for this service (partial refunds? shipped orders? idempotency?), then write the one-paragraph spec you would agree with the interviewer.
followups.repository_exploration: In 10 minutes, draw the call path of OrderService.place_order: which module owns stock, which owns money, which owns storage, and where an exception can leave state half-changed. Write it as five bullet points.
followups.ai_instructions: Write the prompt you would give Claude Code to add a 'max 3 open orders per customer' rule: name the files, the exception to raise, the tests to add, and ask it to show a diff before applying. Compare it with the prompts in your transcript.
followups.verification: Take one change your assistant made today and write two tests that would fail if it were subtly wrong (for example an off-by-one in retries or pagination). Run them against the starter code to prove they catch the bug.
followups.correctness: Write a table of edge cases for list_orders (empty store, exact multiple of the page size, customer filter, bad token, limit 0 and 101) and turn each row into a test.
followups.testing: Add a regression test for each bug you fixed, then run it against a fresh starter (Reset in the dashboard on a copy) to confirm every test fails there and passes on your fix.
followups.code_quality: Refactor place_order so stock reservation and rollback live in one helper with a single responsibility, keep the tests green, and explain the change in three sentences.
followups.communication: Record a 2-minute explanation of how your idempotency works, including one tradeoff (memory growth, key expiry, or payload comparison) and what you would do in production.
